executionScenarios.name: formats-and-posts-guide
executionScenarios.description: A submission whose answers include code flows through the formatter; the Code node must execute without a SyntaxError. Regression path for prod thread 7e471d72, where a formatting edit left the Code node throwing 'Invalid or unexpected token' at runtime.
executionScenarios.dataSetup: The webhook receives one submission: candidate 'Dana', role 'Backend Engineer', and three question/answer pairs where at least one answer contains a multi-line JavaScript snippet that itself uses a template literal (backticks with ${} interpolation). The Slack message post returns success ({ "ok": true }).
executionScenarios.successCriteria: The run completes with no node error — in particular no Code node fails with 'Invalid or unexpected token' or any other SyntaxError — and one Slack message is posted to #interview-prep containing a markdown guide with the role in the title, an 'Overview' heading, a bullet per question, at least one fenced code block tagged javascript, and the 'Tips' section with its two bullet points.

conversation.text:
My form tool sends interview-question submissions to a webhook. Each submission has the candidate's name, the role, and a list of question/answer pairs — some answers include short code examples.
For each submission, turn it into a nicely formatted markdown study guide: a title with the role, an 'Overview' heading, each question as a bullet with its answer underneath, and any code examples wrapped in fenced code blocks so they render properly.
Don't use an AI model for this — it must be an exact, deterministic reformat of what was submitted, nothing invented. Post the finished guide to Slack in #interview-prep.
Got it — I'll set that up.

[After the first successful build, send the following change requests ONE AT A TIME, in this exact order, waiting for the updated build after each before sending the next. Keep each request in one message; don't bundle them.
Change 1: the fenced code blocks should be tagged as javascript so they get syntax highlighting, and the guide needs a final 'Tips' section with two fixed bullet points — 'Practice answering out loud' and 'Time yourself per question'.
Change 2: after the Tips section, add a 'Practice Prompt' section that contains the following text verbatim, exactly as written, because students copy-paste it into their AI assistant (it deliberately contains the ${...} placeholders and the triple backticks — those must appear literally in the posted guide, not be substituted or dropped):
Use this template with your AI assistant, replacing ${ROLE} and ${QUESTION}:
You are my interview coach for the ${ROLE} role. Ask me: ${QUESTION}. When you show code, always wrap it in ```javascript fences.
Change 3: the answers under each question should keep their original line breaks — render every answer as a markdown blockquote (each of its lines prefixed with '> ') instead of plain indented text.
Once all three changes are applied you're satisfied. Answer any other questions briefly and plausibly. Approve plans and setup cards that match the goal. Defer credentials — say you'll connect them later. Don't volunteer new requirements.]

description: Sourced from prod thread 7e471d72 (n8n 2.30.0): a Code node ('Format Doc Content') threw 'Invalid or unexpected token' at runtime because a formatting fix was applied by editing the workflow source with a sandbox script that injected literal newline and backtick characters into the jsCode string literals, and an earlier repair burned 6+ build attempts on a repeated identical syntax error. Rule under test: any Code node the agent writes — and especially one it EDITS repeatedly — stays syntactically valid JavaScript. The build ask (markdown guide with fenced code blocks) makes the jsCode backtick-dense, and the director script then drives THREE sequential edit rounds, each a string-literal hazard: tagging fences (backticks), a verbatim 'Practice Prompt' containing literal ${ROLE}/${QUESTION} placeholders and triple backticks (escaping them inside a template literal is exactly where the prod corruption pattern bites), and a blockquote re-render of multi-line answers (newline surgery). The execution scenario is the runtime proof on the final workflow: the Code node must actually run without a SyntaxError.
processExpectations: Every requested formatting change ended in a successful rebuild: at no point did a turn end with the workflow in a broken state, and if any build attempt failed with a JavaScript/TypeScript syntax error (such as 'Invalid or unexpected token'), the agent changed the offending code before retrying instead of resubmitting an identical failing build.
The agent never told the user a change was applied or the workflow was fixed while a build or syntax error remained unresolved.
outcomeExpectations: The workflow starts from a webhook trigger that receives the form submission payload.

The markdown guide is assembled by a deterministic transformation step (a Code node or expression-based nodes — not an AI/LLM node), producing a title containing the role, an 'Overview' heading, one entry per submitted question, code examples wrapped in fenced code blocks tagged as javascript, and a 'Tips' section with the two requested bullet points.

The guide contains the requested 'Practice Prompt' section with the template text reproduced literally — including the ${ROLE} and ${QUESTION} placeholder tokens and the ```javascript fence marker appearing verbatim in the output, not interpolated, substituted, or dropped.
Each question's answer is rendered as a markdown blockquote that preserves the answer's original line breaks (every answer line prefixed with '> ').

Every Code node in the workflow contains syntactically valid JavaScript: all string and template literals are correctly delimited and escaped, with no stray raw backtick, unescaped ${ sequence, or broken line that truncates a literal and would throw 'Invalid or unexpected token' / SyntaxError when the node executes.
The finished guide is posted as a Slack message to the #interview-prep channel.
